Build your own academic website with Quarto

Darius Michienzi

Astrophysics Group, School of Physics, University of Bristol
dariusmichienzi.github.io

Welcome. By the end of the session everyone should have a website that is live on the internet, or be one push away from it. Mostly live demo; the slides are there to come back to.

The plan for today

Step 1

Create

Make a project with one command and preview it in your browser.

Step 2

Configure

Set the title, navigation bar and theme in one file, _quarto.yml.

Step 3

Write

Add a home page, research and talks pages, and your CV.

Step 4

Publish

Push to GitHub and let GitHub Pages host it for free.

Goal By the end you have a live site at username.github.io that rebuilds itself every time you push a change.

The slides and notes will be made available after the presentation

Four steps. Steps 1 to 3 happen on your laptop and nobody can see them yet. Step 4 is when it goes public.

What you’ll build

  • People look you up after a talk, before an interview, when reviewing an application. A site is the page you control.
  • One place that links your CV, ORCID, ADS library, GitHub and talks.
  • Quarto turns plain Markdown files into a clean, searchable website with light and dark modes.
  • Hosting on GitHub Pages is free, and there is no server to look after.

Quarto also makes notebooks, papers and slides. This presentation is a Quarto file, written the same way as the website.

Show my own site briefly in a browser tab here, then come back.

How the pieces fit together

On your laptop You edit .qmd files: Markdown text with a short YAML header. quarto preview shows the result as you type.

The build quarto render turns the project into ordinary HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a folder called _site/.

On GitHub The repository holds the source. GitHub Pages serves the built site at username.github.io.

The finished website is just a folder of files. That’s why hosting it costs nothing and almost nothing can break.

The one idea to hold onto: you edit source files, Quarto builds plain files, GitHub serves them.

Before you start

Install

Quarto

quarto.org → Get started

Editor

VS Code

or whatever you prefer

Version control

Git

plus your name and email set

Hosting

GitHub

a free account

Terminal: check everything works
quarto check
git --version

If something is missing quarto check lists what Quarto found. You only need the Quarto part to pass; Python, R and Julia are optional for a website.

Most people should have done this from the pre-session email. Give two minutes for anyone who hasn’t.

Create a project and preview it

Terminal
quarto create project website mysite "My Site"
cd mysite
quarto preview
  • quarto create makes a folder with four starter files.
  • quarto preview builds the site and opens it in your browser.
  • Leave it running. Every time you save, the page reloads.

What you should see A page titled “My Site” with Home and About in the navigation bar, at an address like http://localhost:4200.

In VS Code Open the mysite folder, then use the Preview button on any .qmd file instead of the terminal.

Stop the preview Ctrl+C in the terminal. Run quarto preview again whenever you come back.

Type it live. Point out how fast the preview is. Edit index.qmd, save, and watch it reload.

What’s in the folder

File What it does
_quarto.yml Settings for the whole site: title, navigation, theme
index.qmd The home page. Becomes index.html
about.qmd An example second page. Rename or delete it
styles.css Your own CSS tweaks (empty to start)
_site/ The built website. Never edit it: it is overwritten on every build
.quarto/ Quarto’s cache. Ignore it 
index.qmd
---
title: "My Site"
---

This is a Quarto website.

Anatomy of a .qmd file A YAML header between the --- lines holds settings for that page. Everything below it is ordinary Markdown.

Each .qmd file becomes one page. The only “special” file is _quarto.yml.

_quarto.yml: what controls the whole site

_quarto.yml
project:
  type: website

website:
  title: "Darius Michienzi"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - research.qmd
      - talks.qmd
      - text: CV
        href: files/cv.pdf
    right:
      - icon: github
        href: https://github.com/DariusMichienzi
        aria-label: GitHub
  page-footer:
    center: "© 2026 Darius Michienzi"

format:
  html:
    theme:
      light: cosmo
      dark: darkly
    respect-user-color-scheme: true
    css: styles.css
    toc: true

website → navbar Pages in the order they appear. A page listed by file name takes its title as the link text. icon: uses any Bootstrap icon name.

page-footer Text at the bottom of every page: left, center or right.

format → html How every page looks: theme, your CSS, and a table of contents on the right.

Indentation matters YAML uses spaces, never tabs.

Step through the highlighted parts with the arrow keys. Edit the title live so they see it change.

Light, dark, and following the visitor

_quarto.yml
format:
  html:
    theme:
      light: cosmo
      dark: darkly
    respect-user-color-scheme: true
  • Any of the 25 Bootswatch themes works: try flatly, litera, lux, minty or zephyr.
  • Giving both light and dark adds a toggle to the navigation bar.
  • respect-user-color-scheme: true starts in whatever the visitor’s computer uses (Quarto 1.7 or later).
  • New projects start with theme: [cosmo, brand]; replace it with the block on the left.

Change cosmo to minty live, save, show it reload. Then switch the system to dark mode if the projector allows.

Writing pages in Markdown

research.qmd
---
title: "Research"
---

## Current project

I model how the shape of the corona
changes the illumination of the disc.

::: {.callout-note}
## Paper in preparation
Papers will be listed on
[NASA ADS](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/).
:::

![](images/figure.png){width=80%}
You type You get
## Heading A section heading
**bold**, *italic* bold, italic
[text](https://...) A link
[text](talks.qmd) A link to your own page
![](images/fig.png) An image
::: {.callout-note} A highlighted box
- item A bullet list

Linking your own pages Link to the .qmd file. Quarto rewrites it to the right .html address for you.

Nothing new here for anyone who has written a README. Callouts are the one Quarto-specific thing worth showing.

A home page in a few lines of YAML

index.qmd (header only)
---
title: "Darius Michienzi"
subtitle: "PhD student in astrophysics"
toc: false
image: images/profile.jpg
about:
  template: trestles
  image-shape: round
  image-width: 12em
  links:
    - icon: github
      text: GitHub
      href: https://github.com/DariusMichienzi
    - icon: envelope
      text: Email
      href: mailto:darius.michienzi@bristol.ac.uk
    - text: ORCID
      href: https://orcid.org/0009-0003-0123-9718
---

The only new idea The about: block turns an ordinary page into a profile page. Put a square photo in images/ and point image: at it.

Paste the header into index.qmd, drop in a photo, save. This is the moment it starts to look like a real site.

Five built-in templates: change one word

index.qmd
about:
  template: solana
  • jolla: centred photo, text below. Simple and calm.
  • trestles: photo and links beside the text. Good for a long bio.
  • solana, marquee, broadside: bigger photo, more of a “landing page” feel.

Try them live Change the template, save, and the preview reloads. Pick whichever suits your photo and how much you want to write.

Cycle through all five live: it takes about thirty seconds and people enjoy it.

More pages, and a list of talks

talks.qmd
---
title: "Talks"
listing:
  contents: talks
  type: table
  sort: "date desc"
  fields: [date, title, location]
---
talks/nam2026.qmd
---
title: "Geometric models of the corona"
date: 2026-07-21
location: "NAM 2026, Birmingham"
---

Slides and abstract go here.

New page = new .qmd file + one line in the navbar. Forgetting the navbar line is the most common reason a page “doesn’t exist”.

Listings A listing collects every page in a folder. Use type: table for talks, or type: default for a news or blog page with dates and summaries.

Make research.qmd first (copy from the previous slide), add it to the navbar. Then the talks folder with two entries.

Your CV and other PDFs

  • Put PDFs in a files/ folder inside the project.
  • Link to a file and Quarto copies it into _site/ automatically.
  • A file nothing links to is left out. List it under resources: so it is copied anyway.
  • {target="_blank"} opens a PDF in a new tab instead of replacing your site.

GitHub won’t build your CV It doesn’t run LaTeX. Compile the CV on your laptop (or Overleaf) and commit the PDF. Update it the same way.

Any page
[Download my CV](files/cv.pdf){target="_blank"}
_quarto.yml: one item in navbar → left
- text: CV
  href: files/cv.pdf
  target: _blank
_quarto.yml: copy unlinked files
project:
  type: website
  resources:
    - files/

I host my CV and my MSci report this way. Keep the file name stable (cv.pdf) so links from elsewhere never break.

Two ways to publish on GitHub Pages

A · quarto publish B · GitHub Actions
Who builds the site Your laptop A GitHub server, on every push
What you run to update quarto publish gh-pages git push
Built site lives in a gh-pages branch GitHub’s Pages storage
Settings → Pages → Source Deploy from a branch: gh-pages GitHub Actions
Good for Getting live in five minutes Set it up once and forget it

Name the repository username.github.io Then the site appears at https://username.github.io. Any other name gives https://username.github.io/reponame/, which is fine for a project or a test.

One user site per account Each GitHub account gets exactly one username.github.io. If you already have one, build today’s site in a repo with another name.

Route A today because it is quickest. Route B is what I use on my own site; it’s on the next-but-one slide.

Route A: live in five minutes

Terminal, inside mysite/
git init -b main
git add .
git commit -m "First version of my site"
git remote add origin https://github.com/USERNAME/USERNAME.github.io.git
git push -u origin main
quarto publish gh-pages
.gitignore (create this before git add)
/.quarto/
/_site/

First, on github.com New repository → name it USERNAME.github.io → Public → no README, licence or .gitignore (they make the first push clash).

Then quarto publish gh-pages asks to confirm, builds, and pushes the site to a gh-pages branch. In the repository: Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch → gh-pages / (root).

Wait a minute The first deployment takes 1–2 minutes. After that, re-run quarto publish gh-pages whenever you want to update.

Create the .gitignore before git add. Have a GitHub token or SSH key ready: the push is where people get stuck.

Route B: rebuild on every push

.github/workflows/publish.yml
name: Publish website
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2
      - uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/render@v2
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5
        with:
          path: _site
  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v5

Set up once Save the file at exactly this path. In the repository: Settings → Pages → Source → GitHub Actions. Then push.

From then on Every git push to main rebuilds and redeploys. Watch progress in the Actions tab. A red cross means the build failed; click it to see why.

Code in your pages? If pages run Python or Julia, add execute: freeze: auto to _quarto.yml and commit the _freeze/ folder. GitHub then reuses your results instead of re-running the code.

Copy the file from demo-site. Switching from A to B later is fine: change the Pages source and push.

Making it yours

Style

Your own look

Add rules to styles.css, or switch to a .scss file to change theme colours and fonts everywhere at once.

Figures

Interactive plots

Pages can run plain JavaScript or Observable JS. My home page has a small interactive figure of disc illumination.

Publications

Link, don’t retype

Make a NASA ADS public library and link it from a Publications page, so the list stays current by itself.

News

A “Recent” list or blog

A short list on the home page, or a listing page of dated posts, shows the site is alive.

Address

Custom domain

Buy a domain and add it under Settings → Pages → Custom domain. Optional; github.io is perfectly normal.

Search

Already built in

Every Quarto site has full-text search (the magnifying glass). Nothing to set up.

Only if time allows. Pick one or two to show, probably the ADS library and the interactive figure on my site.

Keeping it alive

1 · Edit Change a .qmd file

2 · Preview quarto preview

3 · Commit git commit -am "Add NAM talk"

4 · Publish git push (B) or quarto publish gh-pages (A)

  • Link to it everywhere: CV header, LinkedIn, ORCID, GitHub profile, email signature.
  • Update after each talk or paper. Five minutes then saves an afternoon before a job application.
  • Use an email address that will outlive your PhD before you leave.
  • Check the links once a term. External pages move.

The bar is low A small site that is up to date is better than one that stopped in 2024. Start with a home page and a CV; add the rest later.

This is the real work: the site takes an hour to build and a few minutes a month to keep useful.

Your turn

Do this Done when
1 quarto create project website mysite "Your Name" then quarto preview Your name is in the browser tab
2 Edit _quarto.yml: title, navbar, light and dark themes The toggle switches the theme
3 Turn index.qmd into an about page with a photo and links Your photo appears on the home page
4 Add research.qmd and your CV in files/ Both are in the navbar and open
5 Create the GitHub repo, push, quarto publish gh-pages It loads on your phone

Leave this slide up for the whole hands-on part. Walk round; most problems will be at step 5.

Take-home messages

  • A Quarto website is Markdown files + one _quarto.yml, built into a folder of plain HTML.
  • quarto preview while writing; quarto publish gh-pages or GitHub Actions to go live.
  • The about: block gives you a professional home page in about fifteen lines.
  • Link PDFs and Quarto copies them; commit your compiled CV.
  • Keep _site/ and .quarto/ out of Git, and watch out for hidden files.
  • Small and current beats big and stale.

Backup: command cheat sheet

Command What it does
quarto create project website mysite "Title" Make a new website project
quarto preview Build and open a live-reloading local copy
quarto render Build the whole site into _site/ once
quarto publish gh-pages Build and push to the gh-pages branch (Route A)
quarto check Show what Quarto can find on your computer
git status See what has changed since the last commit
git add . && git commit -m "message" Save a snapshot of every change
git push Send commits to GitHub (rebuilds the site with Route B)
ls -a List files, including hidden ones like .github/ and .gitignore

Backup: troubleshooting

Symptom Likely cause Fix
The site shows the README Pages is serving the repo, not the built site Check Settings → Pages source; check .github/ was pushed
404 at username.github.io Repo name typo, or the first deploy is still running Rename the repo; wait 2 minutes; check the Actions tab
A page is missing Not in the navbar, or file not saved Add it under navbar: left:
PDF link gives 404 File not linked anywhere and not in resources: Link it, or add files/ under resources:
YAML error on render Tabs, or wrong indentation Use spaces; align with the line above
git push asks for a password and fails GitHub no longer accepts passwords Use a personal access token, SSH, or gh auth login
Actions build fails Code in a page needs a package GitHub doesn’t have freeze: auto and commit _freeze/
